{{Short description|Ring homomorphism from the cobordism ring of manifolds to another ring}}
[[File:Cobordism.svg|thumb|A cobordism (''W''; ''M'', ''N'').]]
In [[mathematics]], a '''genus of a multiplicative sequence''' is a [[ring homomorphism]] from the [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] of smooth [[Closed manifold|compact manifold]]s up to the equivalence of bounding a smooth manifold with boundary (i.e., up to suitable [[cobordism]]) to another ring, usually the [[rational number]]s, having the property that they are constructed from a [[sequence]] of polynomials in [[characteristic classes]] that arise as coefficients in formal [[power series]] with good multiplicative properties.

==Definition==
A '''genus''' <math>\varphi</math> assigns a number <math>\Phi(X)</math> to each manifold ''X'' such that
# <math>\Phi(X \sqcup Y) = \Phi(X) + \Phi(Y)</math> (where <math>\sqcup</math> is the disjoint union);
# <math>\Phi(X \times Y) = \Phi(X)\Phi(Y)</math>;
# <math>\Phi(X) = 0</math>  if ''X'' is the boundary of a manifold with boundary. 

The manifolds and manifolds with boundary may be required to have additional structure; for example, they might be oriented, spin, stably complex, and so on (see [[list of cohomology theories#Bordism and cobordism theories|list of cobordism theories]] for many more examples). The value <math>\Phi(X)</math> is in some ring, often the ring of rational numbers, though it can be other rings such as <math>\Z/2\Z</math> or the [[ring of modular forms]].

The conditions on <math>\Phi</math>  can be rephrased as saying that <math>\Phi</math> is a ring homomorphism from the cobordism ring of manifolds (with additional structure) to another ring. 

Example: If <math>\Phi(X)</math> is the [[Signature (topology)|signature]] of the oriented manifold ''X'', then <math>\Phi</math> is a genus from oriented manifolds to the [[ring of integers]].

==The genus associated to a formal power series==
{{main|Multiplicative sequence}}
A sequence of polynomials <math>K_1, K_2,\ldots</math> in variables <math>p_1, p_2,\ldots</math> is called '''multiplicative''' if

:<math>1 + p_1z + p_2z^2 + \cdots = (1 + q_1z + q_2z^2 + \cdots) (1 + r_1z + r_2z^2 + \cdots)</math> 

implies that

:<math>\sum_j K_j(p_1, p_2, \ldots)z^j = \sum_j K_j (q_1, q_2, \ldots) z^j\sum_k K_k (r_1, r_2, \ldots)z^k</math>

If <math>Q(z)</math> is a [[formal power series]] in ''z'' with [[constant term]] 1, we can define a multiplicative sequence 

:<math>K = 1+ K_1 + K_2 + \cdots</math> 

by 

:<math>K(p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots) = Q(z_1)Q(z_2)Q(z_3)\cdots</math>,

where <math>p_k</math> is the ''k''th [[elementary symmetric function]] of the indeterminates <math>z_i</math>. (The variables <math>p_k</math> will often in practice be [[Pontryagin class]]es.)

The genus <math>\Phi</math> of [[Compact space|compact]], [[Connected space|connected]], [[Differentiable manifold|smooth]], [[Orientability|oriented]] manifolds corresponding to ''Q'' is given by

:<math>\Phi(X) = K(p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots)</math>

where the <math>p_k</math> are the [[Pontryagin class]]es of ''X''. The power series ''Q'' is called the '''characteristic power series''' of the genus <math>\Phi</math>. A theorem of [[René Thom]], which states that the rationals tensored with the cobordism ring is a polynomial algebra in generators of degree 4''k'' for positive integers ''k'', implies that this gives a [[bijection]] between formal power series ''Q'' with rational coefficients and leading coefficient 1, and genera from oriented manifolds to the rational numbers.

==L genus==
The '''L genus''' is the genus of the formal power series 

:<math>{\sqrt{z}\over \tanh(\sqrt z)} = \sum_{k\ge 0} \frac{2^{2k}B_{2k}z^k}{(2k)!} = 1 + {z \over 3} - {z^2 \over 45} + \cdots</math>

where the numbers <math>B_{2k}</math> are the [[Bernoulli number]]s. The first few values are: 

:<math>\begin{align}
  L_0 &= 1 \\
  L_1 &= \tfrac13 p_1 \\
  L_2 &= \tfrac1{45}\left(7p_2 - p_1^2\right) \\
  L_3 &= \tfrac1{945}\left(62 p_3 - 13 p_1 p_2 + 2 p_1^3\right) \\
  L_4 &= \tfrac1{14175}\left(381 p_4 - 71 p_1 p_3 - 19 p_2^2 + 22 p_1^2 p_2 - 3 p_1^4\right)
\end{align}</math>

(for further ''L''-polynomials see <ref>McTague, Carl (2014) [http://www.mctague.org/carl/blog/2014/01/05/computing-L-polynomials/ "Computing Hirzebruch L-Polynomials"].</ref> or {{OEIS2C|id=A237111}}). Now let ''M'' be a closed smooth oriented manifold of dimension 4''n'' with [[Pontrjagin class]]es <math>p_i = p_i(M)</math>. [[Friedrich Hirzebruch]] showed that the ''L'' genus of ''M'' in dimension 4''n'' evaluated on the [[fundamental class]] of <math>M</math>, denoted <math>[M]</math>, is equal to <math>\sigma(M)</math>, the [[signature (topology)|signature]] of ''M'' (i.e., the signature of the [[Intersection theory#Topological intersection form|intersection form]] on the 2''n''th cohomology group of ''M''):

:<math>\sigma(M) = \langle L_n(p_1(M), \ldots, p_n(M)), [M]\rangle</math>. 

This is now known as the '''[[Hirzebruch signature theorem]]''' (or sometimes the '''Hirzebruch index theorem'''). 

The fact that <math>L_2</math> is always integral for a smooth manifold was used by [[John Milnor]] to give an example of an 8-dimensional [[piecewise linear manifold|piecewise linear (PL) manifold]] with no [[smooth structure]]. Pontryagin numbers can also be defined for PL manifolds, and Milnor showed that his PL manifold had a non-integral value of <math>p_2</math>, and so was not smoothable.

=== Application on K3 surfaces ===
Since projective [[Pontryagin class#Pontryagin classes on a Quartic K3 Surface|K3 surfaces]] are smooth [[Complex manifold|complex manifolds]] of dimension two, their only non-trivial [[Pontryagin class]] is <math>p_1</math> in <math>H^4(X)</math>. It can be computed as -48 using the tangent sequence and comparisons with complex [[Chern class|Chern classes]]. Since <math>L_1 = -16</math>, we have its signature. This can be used to compute its intersection form as a [[unimodular lattice]] since it has <math>\operatorname{dim}\left(H^2(X)\right) = 22 </math>, and using the classification of unimodular lattices.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Huybrechts|first=Daniel|author-link=Daniel Huybrechts|url=https://www.math.uni-bonn.de/people/huybrech/K3Global.pdf|title=Lectures on K3 Surfaces|pages=285|chapter=14.1 Existence, uniqueness, and embeddings of lattices}}</ref>

==Todd genus==
The '''Todd genus''' is the genus of the formal power series 

:<math>\frac{z}{1 - \exp(-z)} = \sum_{i=0}^\infty\frac{B_i}{i!}z^i</math>

with <math>B_i</math> as before, Bernoulli numbers. The first few values are 

:<math>\begin{align}
  Td_0 &= 1 \\
  Td_1 &= \frac1{2} c_1 \\
  Td_2 &= \frac1{12} \left (c_2 + c_1^2 \right ) \\
  Td_3 &= \frac1{24} c_1 c_2 \\
  Td_4 &= \frac1{720} \left(-c_1^4 + 4 c_2 c_1^2 + 3c_2^2 + c_3 c_1 - c_4\right)
\end{align}</math>

The Todd genus has the particular property that it assigns the value 1 to all complex projective spaces (i.e. <math>\mathrm{Td}_n(\mathbb{CP}^n) = 1</math>), and this suffices to show that the Todd genus agrees with the arithmetic genus for [[Algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]] as the [[arithmetic genus]] is also 1 for complex projective spaces. This observation is a consequence of the [[Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem]], and in fact is one of the key developments that led to the formulation of that theorem.

==Â genus==
The '''Â genus''' is the genus associated to the characteristic power series

:<math>
  Q(z) = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{z}}{\sinh\left(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{z}\right)}
       = 1 - \frac{z}{24} + \frac{7z^2}{5760} - \cdots
</math>

(There is also an A genus which is less commonly used, associated to the characteristic series <math>Q(16z)</math>.) The first few values are

:<math>\begin{align}
  \hat{A}_0 &=  1 \\
  \hat{A}_1 &= -\tfrac1{24}p_1 \\
  \hat{A}_2 &=  \tfrac1{5760}\left(-4p_2 + 7 p_1^2\right) \\
  \hat{A}_3 &=  \tfrac1{967680}\left(-16p_3 + 44p_2 p_1 - 31 p_1^3\right) \\
  \hat{A}_4 &=  \tfrac1{464486400}\left(-192p_4 + 512 p_3 p_1 + 208p_2^2 - 904p_2 p_1^2 + 381p_1^4\right)
\end{align}</math>

The Â genus of a [[spin manifold]] is an integer, and an even integer if the dimension is 4 mod 8 (which in dimension 4 implies [[Rochlin's theorem]]) – for general manifolds, the Â genus is not always an integer. This was proven by [[Friedrich Hirzebruch|Hirzebruch]] and [[Armand Borel]]; this result both motivated and was later explained by the [[Atiyah–Singer index theorem]], which showed that the Â genus of a spin manifold is equal to the index of its [[Dirac operator]].

By combining this index result with a [[Weitzenbock formula]] for the Dirac Laplacian, [[André Lichnerowicz]] deduced that if a compact spin manifold admits a metric with positive [[scalar curvature]], its Â genus must vanish. This only gives an obstruction to positive scalar curvature when the dimension is a multiple of 4, but [[Nigel Hitchin]] later discovered an analogous <math>\Z_2</math>-valued obstruction in dimensions 1 or 2 mod 8. These results are essentially sharp. Indeed, [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Mikhail Gromov]], [[H. Blaine Lawson]], and Stephan Stolz later proved that the Â genus and Hitchin's <math>\Z_2</math>-valued analog are the only obstructions to the existence of positive-scalar-curvature metrics on simply-connected spin manifolds of dimension greater than or equal to 5.

==Elliptic genus==
A genus is called an '''elliptic genus''' if the power series <math>Q(z) = z/f(z)</math> satisfies the condition 

:<math>{f'}^2 = 1 - 2\delta f^2 + \epsilon f^4</math>

for constants <math>\delta</math> and <math>\epsilon</math>. (As usual, ''Q'' is the characteristic power series of the genus.)

One explicit expression for ''f''(''z'') is

:<math>f(z) = \frac{1}{a}\operatorname{sn}\left( az, \frac{\sqrt{\epsilon}}{a^2} \right)</math>

where

:<math>a = \sqrt{\delta + \sqrt{\delta^2 - \epsilon}}</math>

and ''sn'' is the [[Jacobi elliptic function]].

Examples:

*<math>\delta = \epsilon = 1, f(z) = \tanh(z)</math>. This is the L-genus.
*<math>\delta = -\frac{1}{8}, \epsilon = 0, f(z) = 2\sinh\left(\frac{1}{2}z\right)</math>. This is the Â genus.
*<math>\epsilon = \delta^2 , f(z) = \frac{\tanh(\sqrt{\delta}z)}{\sqrt{\delta}}</math>. This is a generalization of the L-genus.

The first few values of such genera are:
:<math>\frac{1}{3}\delta p_1</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{90} \left [ \left (-4\delta^2 +18\epsilon \right )p_2+ \left (7\delta^2-9\epsilon \right )p_1^2\right ]</math>
:<math>\frac{1}{1890} \left [ \left (16\delta^3 + 108\delta \epsilon \right )p_3 + \left (-44\delta^3 +18\delta \epsilon \right )p_2p_1 + \left (31\delta^3 -27\delta \epsilon \right )p_1^3\right ]</math>
<!-- :<math>\frac1{113400}\big[(-192\delta^4 +1728\delta^2\epsilon +1512\epsilon^2)p_4 +(512\delta^4 +432\delta^2\epsilon -1512\epsilon^2)p_3p_1 +(208\delta^4 -1872\delta^2\epsilon + 1512\epsilon^2)p_2^2 +(-904\delta^4 +1836\delta^2\epsilon -756\epsilon^2)p_2p_1^2 +(381\delta^4 -594\delta^2\epsilon +189\epsilon^2)p_1^4\big]</math>
:<math>\left(-\frac{53}{41580}\delta^3 \epsilon+{\frac{17}{27720}}\delta{\epsilon}^{2}+\frac{73}{106920} \delta^5\right)p_1^5 + \left(\frac{481}{103950}\delta^3 \epsilon-{\frac{29}{11550}}\delta{\epsilon}^{2}-{\frac {1073}{467775}}{\delta}^{5} \right) p_2{p_1}^{3}+ \left( {\frac {244}{155925}}{\delta}^{5}-{\frac {37}{51975}}{\delta}^{3}\epsilon-{\frac {2}{5775}}\delta{\epsilon}^{2} \right) p_3p_1^2 + \left( \left( {\frac {622}{467775}}{\delta}^{5}-{\frac{202}{51975}}{\delta}^{3}\epsilon+{\frac {7}{2475}}\delta{\epsilon}^{2} \right) p_2^2+ \left(-\frac{31}{5775} \delta{\epsilon}^{2}-{\frac{424}{467775}}{\delta}^{5}+{\frac{32}{7425}}{\delta}^{3}\epsilon \right) p_4 \right) p_1+ \left(-{\frac{4}{2475}}{\delta}^{3}\epsilon+{\frac{4}{2475}}\delta{\epsilon}^{2}-{\frac {16}{22275}}{\delta}^{5} \right) p_3p_2+ \left(\frac{8}{10395}{\delta}^{3}\epsilon+{\frac {32}{93555}}{\delta}^{5}+{\frac {34}{3465}}\delta{\epsilon}^{2} \right) p_5</math> -->

Example (elliptic genus for quaternionic [[projective plane]]) :

:<math>\begin{align}
  \Phi_{ell}(HP^2) &= \int_{HP^2}\tfrac1{90}\big[(-4\delta^2 +18\epsilon )p_2+(7\delta^2-9\epsilon )p_1^2\big] \\
                   &= \int_{HP^2}\tfrac1{90}\big[(-4\delta^2 +18\epsilon )(7u^2)+(7\delta^2-9\epsilon )(2u)^2\big] \\
                   &= \int_{HP^2} [u^2 \epsilon ] \\
                   &= \epsilon \int_{HP^2} [u^2] \\
                   &= \epsilon * 1 = \epsilon
\end{align}</math>

Example (elliptic genus for octonionic projective plane, or [[Cayley plane]]):

:<math>\begin{align}
  \Phi_{ell}(OP^2) &= \int_{OP^2}\tfrac1{113400} \left[(-192\delta^4 + 1728\delta^2\epsilon + 1512\epsilon^2)p_4 + (208\delta^4 - 1872\delta^2\epsilon + 1512\epsilon^2)p_2^2\right] \\
                   &= \int_{OP^2}\tfrac1{113400}\big[(-192\delta^4 + 1728\delta^2\epsilon + 1512\epsilon^2)(39u^2) + (208\delta^4 - 1872\delta^2\epsilon + 1512\epsilon^2)(6u)^2\big] \\
                   &= \int_{OP^2}\big[ \epsilon^2 u^2 \big] \\
                   &= \epsilon^2\int_{OP^2} \big[ u^2 \big] \\
                   &= \epsilon^2* 1 = \epsilon^2 \\
                   &= \Phi_{ell}(HP^2) ^2
\end{align}</math>

==Witten genus==
The '''Witten genus''' is the genus associated to the characteristic power series

:<math>Q(z) = \frac{z}{\sigma_L(z)} = \exp\left(\sum_{k\ge 2} {2G_{2k}(\tau)z^{2k}\over(2k)!}\right)</math>

where σ<sub>L</sub> is the [[Weierstrass sigma function]] for the lattice ''L'', and ''G'' is a multiple of an [[Eisenstein series]]. 

The Witten genus of a 4''k'' dimensional compact oriented smooth spin manifold with vanishing first Pontryagin class is a [[modular form]] of weight 2''k'', with integral Fourier coefficients.
